#3339. Thanksgiving Blackouts Leave More Than 400,000 Without Power, Millions at Risk

Millions of Americans could be spending Thanksgiving in the dark ... with powerful storms threatening to knock out electricity for days and throw holiday dinner plans into chaos.

More than 400,000 homes and businesses were already without power Thursday morning, according to PowerOutage.com ... with Virginia and Missouri among the hardest-hit states.

Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.

#3338. How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can quickly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

Millions of Amazon Prime users currently pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other plans cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

Access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

For non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how quickly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

Also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's important to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching shows on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Of course, if you are interested in Prime Day bargains, you can always sign up right before the start of the sale and then cancel your membership after Prime Day is over—but Amazon doesn't always make it easy on you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3337. I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

With the recently launched Genie 4 update, this tool is purportedly even more powerful. It now allows you to request live edits (like "make it snow") and incorporate sound and dialog into your prompts. Google is also promising more realistic physics and natural movements in its renderings.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

It's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees."

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

The best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

That said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

#3334. Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company announced that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies plan to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.

#3333. 10 Greatest Netflix Shows of 2026, Ranked

2026 has been a year of growth and expansion for Netflix. With its intriguing plots, fantastic production, and well-designed characters that leave an impact, Netflix has rolled out several great shows this year. While there has not been a monumental rise in critical quality, the streamer’s lineup of shows has been much stronger and more positive than its original movies.

On the one hand, the streaming service has released multiple fresh new originals like The Boroughs to cure the Stranger Things hangover. At the same time, the year has also seen the returns of acclaimed shows like Beef and Black Doves, which have thrilled fans even more than last time. So, before we close the book on this year, here’s our ranked selection of the top 10 best Netflix shows of 2026.

Based on the American literary classic by Laura Ingalls Wilder, Little House on the Prairie follows the Ingalls family, parents Charles (Luke Bracey) and Caroline (Crosby Fitzgerald), and their daughters, Laura (Alice Halsey) and Mary (Skywalker Hughes), as they move from Wisconsin to a newly developing settlement in Kansas to start a new chapter for the family. Developed by Rebecca Sonnenshine, the Netflix original series marks the third television adaptation of the beloved book series.

Heavily compared to the NBC classic, Little House on the Prairie has had mixed reviews since it premiered in the summer of 2026. The show earned praise for its grounded historical context and sweeping visuals and period-accurate aesthetic, but has also been criticized for lacking the gritty realities of frontier life that the older adaptation captured so well.

Among the first major releases of 2026, Netflix’s Regency-era epic romance drama returned with an all-new fourth season, based on the novel An Offer from a Gentleman, the third in Julia Quinn’s titular novel series. Bridgerton Season 4 follows a classic Cinderella-inspired romance centering on Benedict Bridgerton (Luke Thompson) and Sophie Baek (Yerin Ha).

After a divisive third season, Bridgerton Season 4 was a welcome return for the show, which has become a global streaming sensation since its premiere in 2020. The new chapter brings back the high-stakes, slow-burn romance narrative that has defined Bridgerton as a sensation of modern romance television. Critics and reviewers have praised Bridgerton Season 4 for its emotionally grounded storytelling, compelling romance plot, and better visual aesthetic compared to its previous seasons.

Two years after its first season premiere, The Gentlemen, Guy Ritchie’s black comedy crime drama reboot of his 2019 film returns for an action-packed, explosive second season, as Duke Edward “Eddie” Horniman (Theo James) deepens his grip on this underground cannabis business. As Eddie transforms into a ruthless power player in tandem with Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario) and her father, Bobby (Ray Winstone), he finds himself facing new rivals and the consequences of unlimited ambition.

Though the new season arrived after a two-year gap, The Gentlemen Season 2 makes it worth the wait for fans and offers everything you expect from a Guy Ritchie caper. In fact, the second season of the crime thriller is darker, sharper, sleeker, and more high-stakes than the first. The second season of The Gentlemen trades the lighthearted, absurd tone and style of Season 1 for a punchier, snappier second chapter in Eddie’s evolution, while maintaining the original visual flair and cinematic style.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Lee Sung Jin’s multi-award-winning black comedy anthology returned this year with a second season featuring an all-new cast in a new story of class satire and the unpredictable human condition. Beef Season 2 explores the escalating feud between couples Ashley (Cailee Spaeny) and Austin (Charles Melton), employees at an elite country club, and their boss and his wife, Josh (Oscar Isaac) and Lindsey (Carey Mulligan). After Austin and Ashley see the latter in a questionable confrontation, it sets off a wild story of blackmail, sabotage, and coercion, upending everyone’s lives.

After the raw and unabashed exploration of rage and existential crisis that Beef introduced in its first season, the second season expands to a more philosophical and spiritual exploration of human nature. While the new story does not really match up to the phenomenal success and critical acclaim of the first season, Beef Season 2 anchors itself in the crackling performances of its lead cast and sharp class satire.

Created by Haley Z. Boston, Something Very Bad is Going to Happen is a horror-thriller miniseries that tells the story of a newly engaged couple, Rachel (Camilla Morrone) and Nicky (Adam di Marco), who are all set to get married. In the week leading up to the wedding, Rachel begins to experience several sinister, supernatural events that turn her wedding stress into a dark nightmare, making her seriously question her decision.

One of the most highly anticipated horror series of 2026, Something Very Bad is Going to Happen puts an eerie psychological and supernatural spin on pre-wedding jitters. The dark gothic horror drama has been praised for its atmospheric tone and surreal treatment, which takes inspiration from horror classics like Rosemary’s Baby.

An adaptation of Jo Nesbø’s novels featuring the titular central character, Detective Hole is a gritty Nordic crime drama that follows the homicide detective, a brilliant but troubled man who is in search of a horrific serial killer. Starring Tobias Santelmann as Detective Hole, the series follows his relentless and often dangerous attempts to catch the killer while also trying to bring his corrupt fellow officer, Tom (Joel Kinnaman), to justice.

Directed by Oystein Karlsen and Anna Zackrisson, Detective Hole is a grim but stylish crime thriller with unexpected plot twists that can keep you hooked from start to finish. The Netflix original miniseries joins the long list of Nordic noir thrillers that Netflix has been dishing out over the last few years. Intricate and intense, Jo Nesbø’s Detective Hole is a deeply layered serial killer mystery any genre fan would love.

Debora Cahn’s political thriller series returns for a fourth season that somehow manages to improve upon the first three excellent installments. Keri Russell and Rufus Sewell lead the show as Kate and Hal Wyler, a couple who attempts to juggle a marriage that’s often just as complicated as diplomacy. Things are more complex than ever this time around, as President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) begins making riskier and riskier moves, and a new Prime Minister in the form of Bethan Vaughn (Jodie Whittaker) throws alliances into question.

The Diplomat Season 4 has earned rave reviews from critics, currently holding an impressive 97% on Rotten Tomatoes. Janney’s shocking but well-deserved Emmy win this year seems like it could be the first of many more accolades in the show’s future. Season 4 both tackled the fallout from last season’s jaw-dropping cliffhanger and introduced a new twist in the finale’s last moments; needless to say, Season 5 can’t come soon enough.

Starring Alfred Molina, Geena Davis, Bill Pullman, Alfre Woodard, Clarke Peters, and Denis O’Hare, The Boroughs is a sci-fi adventure involving a group of residents at a retirement community out in the deserts of New Mexico. When a new resident named Sam (Molina) witnesses the shocking death of a fellow retiree and begins investigating, his search leads him to an unearthly, uncanny conspiracy that threatens the lives of the residents in the seemingly perfect community.

Executive produced by the Duffer Brothers and developed by Jeffrey Addis and Will Matthews, The Boroughs is a great follow-up to the Duffers’ five-season sci-fi epic. But the show surpasses its perception of “Stranger Things with older adults” and stands on its own merit as a heartfelt exploration of later-life challenges told as a chilling sci-fi mystery. The series has been widely praised for its standout cast, poignant storytelling, and excellent production values.

Zoe Kazan's East of Eden is undeniably one of the best shows of the year. The adaptation of John Steinbeck's epic 1952 novel, the show centers around the Trasks and the Hamiltons, two families whose lives intersect in California's Salinas Valley. The novel takes heavy inspiration from the story of Cain and Abel, tackling complex themes of good versus evil.

Florence Pugh’s performance as Cathy Ames is widely considered one of the best in her career, which is saying something considering she has everything from Midsommar to Little Women on her resume. The rest of the cast, which includes Christopher Abbott, Mike Faist, Hoon Lee, and Ciarán Hinds, is impressive in their own right. The series earned 6.5 million views in its first four days alone and only increased in popularity over time, solidifying itself as one of the year’s most enduring hits.

Joe Barton’s genre-bending spy thriller returned this year after a two-year interval for a brand-new season with Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw reprising their roles as spies from the titular agency, Helen and Sam, respectively. In Black Doves Season 2, the duo faces new threats after discovering a conspiracy involving their handler, Reed (Sarah Lancashire). At the same time, Helen finds herself on increasingly uncertain ground after her husband becomes the Prime Minister. The new season also adds Ambika Mod, Neve Campbell, Babou Ceesay, and Samuel Barnett to the cast.

Black Doves Season 2 has proved itself to be darker, sharper, and faster than the first season, with higher stakes and a higher comedic quotient. While the new season successfully maintains the show’s original themes of love, friendship, and espionage, it arguably lacks the moodiness and charm of classic British spy thrillers, which Season 1 achieved excellently. Despite that, Black Doves Season 2 has earned rave reviews, surpassing the acclaim of the previous season, with critics praising the more grounded plotlines and Knightley and Whishaw’s chemistry.

Rats don't hibernate during the winter months, instead they desperately seek out warm shelter. And while there's one thing you should clear from your yard to prevent rats, you should also be focused on your shed.

It's the perfect spot for rats to take up residence and once they find somewhere they like, they'll stick around and populate. So, before you end up with a rat infestation in your shed, here's the 3 things I recommend doing every winter to make sure they stay out (and stay away from your home, too).

Rats can fit into holes as small as a quarter, so if you've got any gaps around your shed, they'll be sure to find a way in. And if they don't find an appropriate hole, they might chew one of their own to gain access. So, what I like to do every winter is a thorough check of the exterior and interior of my shed looking for any holes.

If you find any, it also matters what you seal the gap with, as they may just break their way through something too flimsy.

For this, I recommend using a steel wool or wire mesh. If you notice they're digging underneath, it might also be worth laying some concrete slabs or gravel around these areas, too.

Steel wool is great for filling holes and blocking gaps around your shed. Then, the rats won't be able to chew through, creating the perfect barrier to keep them out. It can be used for both indoor and outdoor filling and can be easily cut to size with scissors. With this 2-Pack, you'll get 3" x 10ft coverage.

The problem with rats moving into your shed is that once they're there, you'll likely need to call in pest control to get them out. If you try and deal with it yourself by going in and moving things around, you might encourage the rats to move towards your home and into your garden instead.

To prevent this, I like to give my shed a good sort out before winter to make sure there's no places for the rats to hide.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I like to grab a few plastic boxes with lids to store anything in that I might have been leaving discarded on the floor and, if you've got space, shelves are also great for moving things off the floor and keeping them away from gnawing teeth.

While storing any seeds, bulbs or bird food in your shed seems like a good idea, it's not so true in winter. As well as looking for shelter, rats are also looking for food. So, if you have seeds and a shed, they'll more than happily move in.

What I like to do is move all the seeds and anything else the rats might want to eat out of my shed and seal them away inside my home instead. But, if you don't have room, putting these things into stainless steel containers with screw-on lids and leaving them in your shed will keep them away from rats.

With these three simple steps, I've avoided rats year-in-year-out and, hopefully, you will too. Fortunately, doing these tasks is also super affordable and will cost you far less to carry out than calling in pest control.

#3330. 10 Shows Like 'Yellowjackets' You Should Watch Next

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the new social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the big city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their new home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated shows in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

#3329. Aaron Rodgers Blasted By Former Teammate Over 'Despicable' Mike McCarthy Rant

Aaron Rodgers is catching heat from one of his former Green Bay Packers teammates ... with T.J. Lang ripping the quarterback for publicly dragging Mike McCarthy through the mud.

The former NFL offensive lineman unloaded on Rodgers Wednesday on Detroit's 97.1 The Ticket ... calling the QB's comments "despicable" and accusing him of having a "victim mentality."

Lang called out Rodgers for previously criticizing former teammates and coaches for airing their dirty laundry publicly ... only to turn around and do the same thing.

Rodgers went scorched earth on McCarthy Wednesday on "The Pat McAfee Show," accusing the Pittsburgh Steelers head coach of falling asleep during meetings and even mistakenly referring to the Steelers as the Packers.

Rodgers was released by the Steelers Wednesday following the explosive interview.

Lang says he's still close with McCarthy and spoke to him Monday night ... but hasn't spoken to Rodgers in about 5 years and can't remember the last time the QB returned one of his texts.

He also claims other former teammates share his feelings about Rodgers.

The three spent 8 seasons together in Green Bay, winning a Super Bowl in 2011.

#3328. AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

#3327. If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3325. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3324. The Best Part of Spawn’s Christmas Thriller Is Letting Santa Be the Final Girl

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Of all the things I expected to worry about while reading a Christmas slasher set in the Spawn Universe, whether Santa Claus could get a 911 dispatcher to stay on the phone was pretty far down the list. In I Saw Santa, Nicholas finds the Anderson family murdered on Christmas Eve and calls for help. When the dispatcher asks him to say something if he can hear her, he tries to give her the family’s name. From her end, the line is quiet. From his, he gets to hear a perfectly reasonable woman explain why she’s about to hang up on him. It’s a hell of a thing to do to a guy who still has four time zones’ worth of presents to deliver.

When I spoke with Todd McFarlane, Chris Killian, and Andrew Sanders for Collider about I Saw Santa and its sequel, I Saw Spawn #1, Killian explained that the call came out of a question he and Sanders had to answer. “If he knows who the killer is, why is he not warning anybody through all this?” Nicholas does warn people. He writes to the local authorities, contacts Interpol, and even tries the Vatican. His problem is that most adults know exactly what to do with a letter to Santa and have every reason to be suspicious of one that comes from him. Getting on the phone ought to improve his chances, except Killian and Sanders took one familiar piece of Christmas lore at its word. As Killian put it, “If you don’t believe in him, you can’t see him, you can’t hear him. And how horrifying is that for him?”

What gives the 911 call its bite is that the dispatcher is probably pretty good at her job, but the Andersons are no closer to getting help. Artist Thomas Nachlik lets us follow both sides of the conversation on the page: we can read the name Santa gives her, so when she asks him to speak up, there’s a moment where it feels as though all he has to do is say it again. That little bit of hope is worth preserving for as long as she stays on the line. McFarlane brought up John Carpenter’s The Thing when he described how a horror story can make even the prospect of rescue work against its characters. Sometimes, he said, “the cavalry is not coming.”

McFarlane points out that most horror stories tell out that half an hour. Here, Santa gets the length of a phone call, and that was where McFarlane saw another Carpenter movie in Nicholas’ predicament. Killian and Sanders had found something that “basically isolates this horror and puts Santa on his own,” he explained. Once that happens, “now he just becomes Jamie Lee Curtis. Now what do I do?” It’s a fair question to ask of a man whose job requires him to keep visiting houses on the very night a killer knows where to find him. When I suggested they’d made Santa the final girl, Killian laughed: “That was exactly what we did.”

The nastiest part of the entire thing is that Charlie Kohl is one of the few people (who isn't a child) that still believes. He stayed up hoping to catch Santa coming down the chimney and saved everything Nicholas ever brought him. Unfortunately for Santa, what he brought Charlie was coal, and the boy has been looking forward to giving every piece of it back. Killian described the coal as something Nicholas hopes will “help bad children sort of find their way out of the dark.” But this case and probably several others those intentions have been misinterpreted, and Charlie has had years to sit with the knowledge that somebody saw what he did, judged him for it, and would be back at his house next Christmas Eve. Of all the people Santa needs to convince he exists, the one who's kept the receipts is the one he has reason to fear.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Krampus has always been more my speed at Christmas, so one of the pleasures of I Saw Spawn is discovering that he has apparently spent years nursing a grievance over the direction of the family business. In Killian and Sanders’ version of Christmas, Krampus and Santa are brothers, and Nicholas made a fairly consequential decision about what the holiday ought to look like without securing his brother’s vote. As Killian put it, “I think Krampus is actually a little hurt by it," which is understandable considering he's been locked away while his brother went on to become one of the most beloved figures in the world.

What sells their falling-out is that I Saw Santa has already given Krampus an infuriatingly good example to cite. Nicholas spent years leaving coal for Charlie Kohl in the hope that the boy would turn his life around: imagine how that looks to the brother who used to be in charge of dealing with naughty children. Killian had a pretty good handle on the argument Krampus would make in his own defense.

“'Because if I’d been around, you know, eating naughty kids, then this maybe wouldn’t have been a problem.'”

Somewhere in the middle of a perfectly reasonable objection to eating children, Santa now has to concede that his brother has a point about Charlie. That’s a far better use of Krampus than bringing him out at Christmas to give somebody a scare, and it’s also where I Saw Spawn feels most like a sequel worth picking up on its own. The first comic lets us see why Nicholas keeps giving Charlie another chance, and the second gives us somebody who’s known Nicholas long enough to be thoroughly unimpressed by that quality in him. Even the sight of the brothers together raises a question about who got to tell the family story. Killian liked that “Santa looks like a normal guy, and then Krampus is this big giant,” because “there’s something else going on here if these two are related.” That sent me down a rabbit hole during the interview. If these two share a family resemblance, who decided Santa was the normal-looking one? Presumably the same brother who got to keep the holiday, but exploring that is for another series.

Collider exclusively reveals preview pages from ‘I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale’ #2.

By the time Nicholas sends Alberich to find Al Simmons in I Saw Spawn, the elf is following up on a letter Spawn has already read and dismissed. From Santa’s end, he recognizes that now somebody has to deliver the message in person, which is how a centuries-old elf ends up clinging to Spawn’s cape on a rooftop in Rat City. Al’s first reaction, as McFarlane put it, is “Is this a con? Is this a trick? Who’s trying to get me?” Given how often somebody from Hell actually is trying to get him, Al has probably saved his own skin a few times by asking those very questions. But here, it's him who needs to do the saving.

Asked what makes Spawn the man to call when Christmas is in trouble, Killian’s first answer was “the last resort.” Then he added something considerably more tender: “Santa knows all the children.” That includes Al Simmons, a boy Nicholas can remember and a grown man who could introduce himself on the street and be told to his face that Al Simmons is dead. McFarlane saw the appeal for Santa immediately. “That dude understands people not trusting the truth, right?” He also saw the catch:

“The problem is he’s now not gonna trust me.”

That’s my favorite reason to put these two on a rooftop together, even if Santa has to send an elf in his place. Nicholas has spent Christmas Eve asking people to believe something extraordinary about him. With Al, he can finally return the favor. Long before there was a Hellspawn in Rat City, there was a kid whose house Santa knew how to find. After spending an entire comic hoping somebody would pick up the phone for Santa Claus, I’ve rarely wanted a man to open his mail so badly.

I Saw Spawn #1 is available now, while #2 arrives December 16 from Image Comics.

#3320. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3318. 20 of the Coolest Tech Stocking Stuffers for Under $50

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

What if you make this the year you don't fill all the stockings with candy or gift cards? Both have their place, but if you want to make this the best Christmas ever, you have to shove some tech in those stockings. The good news: Tech gifts don’t have to be expensive to be impressive.

No matter who you're shopping for, there are tons of affordable gizmos that are some combination of cool and useful and that feel pricier than they are. Here are 20 cool tech stocking stuffers to light up any holiday morning, all of which cost less than $50.

If there's an old-school gamer on your list, their Christmas morning will be extra merry if it includes a tiny video game emulator. R36T Retro Gaming Console ($48.98) puts over 18,000 video games in the palm of your hand. It has a 3.5" screen, so whether they like arcade classics or consoles-of-the-past, they can fit 'em all in a pocket.

The Xteink X4 is an e-reader that's smaller than your phone. It uses e-ink like an Amazon Kindle, so you can whip a glare-free screen out of your pocket and start reading anywhere there's a light source. The X4 is a no-frills gadget—there's no lighting, touchscreen, or apps—but if you want a cheap, convenient way to read for around $50, it's perfect.

Those disposable cans of compressed air with the red straws are so 2015. Blow the dust off your electronics with an SDFM Electric Air Duster instead. With an engine that moves at 150,000 RPM, it shoots air such high speeds, the dust doesn't stand a chance. It's also cordless and comes with a variety of cleaning attachments to keep your gear in top shape.

If your giftee likes to listen to music or podcasts while drifting off to sleep, the only gift better than a pair of sleep headphones is two pairs of sleep headphones! This two-pack retails for $22.99 and contains two headbands with built in speakers you can pair with your phone or other device easily.

Your giftee may have the tech side of their battle station/home office locked down, but I bet they don't have the aesthetics dialed in. Govee Smart LED Light Bars ($54.99, but currently on sale for $34.99) are programmable, colorful light bars that work with Alexa and Google Assistant and can display light effects created from 16 millions colors. It even syncs with your music to provide trippy visuals.

My lifestyle doesn't involve cutting down trees, but I still need one of these miniature chainsaws. I mean, it's a chainsaw, and it's only six inches long. This Seeii mini chainsaw ($49.99) is battery-powered, so no one will be accidentally cutting the cord. According to the listing, it's suitable for tree pruning, garden artistry, shrub trimming, forest logging, and wood cutting.

You know what computer fiends are missing in their lives? Knobs. This little $33 gadget lets you assign functions to four external knobs and 12 push buttons, so you can finally have a decent volume control, scrub through video smoothly, skip music tracks with a button push, and control any other function easily and physically. Perfect for gamers.

You could use a tape measure like a caveman, or you could measure things with a frickin' laser that fits in your pocket. This $40 gadget has an LED screen that's easy to read and it doubles as a cat toy. But does it measure things? Damn right it measures things—big things, little things, middle-sized things—it doesn't care what you put in front of it, it will measure the hell out of it! (Up to 98 feet, anyway.)

This compact Bluetooth speaker has an Amazon rating of 4.6 stars out of 5, and it's cheap—just $45. It's waterproof, it sounds great, and it features a built-in light show with six different settings so you can check out cool visuals with your tunes.

A single Apple Airtag makes a great gift to accompany the main gift you don't want someone to lose. Or they can put it on their wallet or your keys, and if they misplace them, they can hit a button and it will play a sound while the FindMy app displays a map that leads to the missing item. Plus, it works in reverse, so you can hit a tag and it will ring your lost phone.

If you want to give the gift of warmth for the holidays, you could do a lot worse than this portable neck, shoulder, and back warmer. There are three temperature settings, a safety shut-off feature, and it heats up really fast, for only $33.

This tiny little vacuum from Odistar will keep their desktop dust-free. It sucks with 1000Pa of suction power for 400 minutes off a single charge, and it's very easy to use: You put it in the palm of your hand and push it around. Cool!

It's not like people need an endoscope camera every day, but if the need for a tiny camera does arise—if they need to see why the engine isn't working or if their wedding ring falls behind the oven—they'll be glad to have this Anykit USB Endoscope Camera. It plugs right into an Android or iPhone and captures HD photos and video of places the sun don't shine.

If your giftee is carrying their laptop around to coffeehouses like a chump, this is the perfect present. They can connect a foldable mini Bluetooth keyboard from iClever to their phone, and turn it into an ultra-portable productivity device. It even has a little trackpad!

This skinny extra battery charges a phone magnetically or with a USB-C cable. It's fast, too. It can charge an iPhone 16 Pro Max to 37% in 30 minutes via the USB-C port and it's less than three inches wide.

Projectors have gotten really good and really small over the last few years, and they prices have come down massively too. This mini projector costs only $29 and projects a 720p image up to 120" and it weighs only about two pounds.

Most people already have a media streamer attached to their televisions, but in case you're gifting someone who doesn't, the Roku Streaming Stick 4K is a solid choice in the $50 price range. This no-frills device serves up 4K HD video, gives you access to hundreds of free and premium channels, and is easy to setup.

The Twelve South AirFly SE is an ultra-compact Bluetooth transmitter lets you plug into any device with a 3.5 mm jack, like in-flight entertainment systems, gym machines, or TVs, and stream audio wirelessly to your Bluetooth earbuds or headphones. Leave those accursed wired headphone in the drawer where they belong!

This is an essential gift if there's a cyclist in your life and anyone who wants to maintain proper PSI in their car tires. This portable air compressor weighs less than a pound and is a steal at only $40. It's rechargeable, has an onboard pressure gauge, an LED flashlight, and can inflate a car tire in only eight minutes.

#3316. Brad Pitt's Stylish WWII Spy Thriller Officially Hits Paramount+

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

This has been a terrific year for Brad Pitt, who successfully followed up the biggest hit of his career with two very different films. Last year, Pitt headlined the sports drama F1, which grossed more than $630 million worldwide and scored a Best Picture nomination at the Oscars. It was the biggest hit of his career as a leading man, but Pitt's immediate follow-up was a far riskier bet. The new movie, Heart of the Beast, defied expectations to emerge as a sleeper hit, grossing nearly $200 million worldwide against a reported budget of $82 million. This week, Pitt returned to his Oscar-winning role from Quentin Tarantino's Once Upon a Time in Hollywood in a new sequel that's getting an unusual release from Netflix.

At the same time, fans can also check out one of Pitt's more overlooked original movies, which is currently streaming on Paramount+. But first, a little about The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher and slated for a Netflix release on December 23. The streamer has given the movie a two-week IMAX-exclusive run that began on November 25 ahead of Thanksgiving weekend. The movie is projected to deliver a single-digit haul from 250 IMAX screens at the domestic box office.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth comes on the heels of fellow Netflix movies to get theatrical runs, such as the Spanish-language Oscar contender La Bola Negra and the World War II drama The Mosquito Bowl. Produced on a reported budget of $120 million, the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel marks Fincher's fifth major project with Netflix, after the streaming series House of Cards and Mindhunter, and the movies Mank and The Killer. The new film has received positive early reviews, and is now sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 82% critics' score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes.

Meanwhile, according to FlixPatrol, Heart of the Beast remains one of the most popular movies on the domestic PVOD market two weeks after its digital debut. The survival thriller, directed by David Ayer, holds a "Certified Fresh" 84% critics' score and a "Verified Hot" 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Audiences can also check out Pitt's World War II espionage thriller Allied, which recently turned 10 years old. The movie was directed by Robert Zemeckis and written by Steven Knight, who is also penning the screenplay for the upcoming James Bond reboot starring Robert Pattinson. The movie underperformed at the box office, grossing around $120 million worldwide against a reported budget of more than $100 million, but audiences interested in seeing how Knight navigates an old-fashioned spy narrative can check it out on Paramount+. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3314. Alaska Woman Killed After Walking Into Spinning Plane Propeller at Airport

A horrific scene unfolded at an Alaska airport just 2 days before Thanksgiving ... a woman was killed after walking straight into a plane's spinning propeller.

According to Alaska State Troopers, Christina Blake was driving on a taxiway at Big Lake Airport Tuesday afternoon when a small plane landed. The pilot stopped to give Blake room to move her car ... but instead, she got out, approached the aircraft and walked directly into its spinning propeller.

Police, firefighters and paramedics rushed to the airport shortly before 5 PM ... but Blake was pronounced dead at the scene. The pilot was uninjured.

Here's where things get particularly puzzling ... authorities say Blake had no apparent connection to the pilot, the plane or the airport, and investigators don't believe she intentionally walked into the propeller.

Blake's body was taken to the State Medical Examiner's Office for an autopsy ... and the investigation remains ongoing.
