#3273. An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it …

I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the company did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

So if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The company solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.

Should you buy an automatic espresso machine or a manual espresso machine?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime. There's so much noise online about coffee — grind size, flow rate, milk texture — that I'm surprised any newbies are brave enough to take the plunge and buy their first espresso machine.

But the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy. There are loads of different types of machines for different types of coffee drinkers: superautomatic, semi-automatic, manual, bean-to-cup/all-in-one... the list goes on. Today, let's get to the bottom of it.

What type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy? I'm using Casabrews, Ninja, and De'Longhi espresso machines to exemplify my points today — and they're all on sale for Black Friday.

The De'Longhi Rivelia is my favorite automatic espresso machine. It has two hoppers so you can switch out beans if you so please, and it makes both hot and cold drinks at the push of a button (but you have to buy the cold frother separately, unfortunately).

The Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is like the best of all worlds. It has a built-in grinder and tamping assist to prevent messes, and it has both manual and automatic milk frothing. This machine is great for learning how to be a barista.

There's one key difference between automatic and manual machines: ease of use. (Size and price also come into play!)

Automatic machines are called that for a reason: press a button, and you get hot coffee in seconds.

An automatic coffee machine selection screen generally looks something like this.

Some machines have upwards of 50 recipes. The De'Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499) offers 38 recipes — some of which I, an ex-barista, had never heard of — including hot and cold beverages. At the press of a button, the machine makes your drink for you.

Depending on price, some automatic machines have integrated milk frothing, like the pictured De'Longhi Rivelia ($1,499) or the De'Longhi Magnifica Duo ($999)

You don't have to do anything. No grinding, no tamping, no calculating dosage volume. As long as there are beans in the hopper, water in the tank, and electricity in the machine, it'll take care of everything.

Automatic machines are ideal if you drink a lot of coffee, but either you don't have time to make it yourself, or you don't want to make it yourself. Both are valid.

But what about a manual espresso machine? Manual espresso machines vary in functionality — some have built-in grinders, so closer to automatics, but some are incredibly hands-on. Let's run through a few examples.

This is the Casabrews 3700 Essential. It's the cheapest espresso machine I've rated highly, and my only recommendation for a sub-$100 espresso machine. If you want the cheapest manual espresso machine on the market, I'd go for this one.

This machine necessitates either a separate grinder or getting your coffee ground for espresso at a local cafe. It comes with dual-walled (pressurized) coffee baskets. While a pressurized basket means it doesn't make "technically" perfect espresso, it's a fantastic machine to learn on, as it's incredibly forgiving.

However, you do need to spend a bit of time learning the ropes. Unlike an automatic machine, you have to do everything yourself. You need to grind the coffee, put the coffee in the portafilter, press "start", and steam your milk.

If you want to get into coffee as a hobby, or you like the routine of making coffee, then I would recommend a manual machine such as this.

However, if you want to make your life easier and you have a little more money to spend, I'd also recommend looking at manual espresso machines with built-in grinders, like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

As you can see, this machine has a lot more going on than the Casabrews 3700 Essential. The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus has a built-in grinder (on the left) and tamping assist (also on the left).

Although you still need to put beans in the hopper and adjust grind size yourself, this machine takes a lot of the hassle out of your morning brew. The Luxe Cafe Mini doesn't have automatic milk frothing, but the Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (pictured) does. The Mini will set you back $449, while the Plus goes for $499. Right now, though, the Mini Plus is $419, and the Mini is $399.

The long and short of it is this: No time to spend making coffee? Just want coffee, stat? Automatic — De'Longhi Rivelia.

Want to learn the art of coffee, and don't mind buying a grinder or getting your beans ground at a cafe? Manual — Casabrews 3700 Essential.

Still want to make the coffee yourself, but you want a built-in grinder? Manual with a built-in grinder — Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

Although not as integral as ease of use, size is also something to consider. In general, automatic machines are pretty huge. Here's a size comparison of our three case studies.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (manual, grinder)

Casabrews 3700 Essential (manual, no grinder)

If you're short on space, the answer's kind of obvious — it should probably be a manual with no grinder. However, you need to remember you will either require a separate grinder or have to get your beans ground at a cafe.

Obviously, though, automatic machines are much larger than manuals. I would only recommend automatics if you're sure you have the space for them — they look bigger and bulkier than the numbers might suggest.

For everyone in between, I'd go for the Ninja.

Obviously, the more features a machine has, the higher its price. In general, automatic machines will set you back at least $1,000 — the only models I've tested under this are the $999 De'Longhi Magnifica Duo and the $999 Jura ENA4 — the latter of which can't make milk drinks. Honestly, what's the point? If you like black coffee, just get a drip machine like the Moccamaster KBGV Select ($270 right now on Black Friday deal).

After automatic machines come manual machines with built-in grinders. This price can range from $3,000 (Breville Oracle Dual Boiler) to $229 (Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder). As someone who's tested all the cheapest models and all the high-end models, I would be wary of a machine charging less than $400. I'd recommend machines like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini (pictured, $499), Breville Barista Express ($699), and De'Longhi Arte Evo ($699) — the latter of which can make cold(ish) brew!

I want you to answer these three questions.

What did you get? Here are my top recommendations for each type.

Depending on your quiz results, I'd recommend one of these three machines. Let me know which one you go for in the comments — I'd love to hear about it!

The De'Longhi Rivelia is my favorite automatic espresso machine. It has two hoppers so you can switch out beans if you so please, and it makes both hot and cold drinks at the push of a button (but you have to buy the cold frother separately, unfortunately).

The Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is like the best of all worlds. It has a built-in grinder and tamping assist to prevent messes, and has both manual and automatic milk frothing. This machine is great to learn how to be a barista on.

While you can find plenty of deals on older headphone models during Black Friday sales, it’s rare to see a record-low price and a nearly 30% discount on newer, highly rated models from top brands. That’s exactly why this deal on the critically praised Beats 360 headphones should be on your radar. They’re now down to $249 (originally $349.99) in Amazon’s early Black Friday sale.

With a design that looks like the love child of the AirPods Max and the Beats Studio Pro, these have an adjustable telescoping frame and a unique modular design that lets you mix and match ear pad colors. The color-swapping bundle isn’t currently on sale, but it’s reassuring to know you can replace the ear pads as they wear out.

They’re controlled by two buttons on each earcup and powered by a dedicated Beats chip, with support for both Android devices and iPhones. You can switch noise modes and, on an iPhone, activate features like Personalized Spatial Audio in Settings. They last up to 32 hours with ANC on, which is longer than both the more expensive Sony WH-1000XM6 and AirPods Max 2.

According to Beats, the 360 offer up to 1.75 times the noise cancellation of the Beats Studio Pro. PCMag’s review, which gave the headphones an “Excellent” rating, was impressed by how well they blocked out everything from plane engine noise to café chatter. #3269. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3268. All the ‘GTA’ Games Ever, Ranked

Unless you’ve been locked in a bank vault somewhere for the last 30 years, there’s a good chance that you’ve heard of Grand Theft Auto. Originally launched for PC and PlayStation in 1997, the series began as a solid commercial success for fans of edgy humor and shooters, before becoming a pop culture phenomenon in the early 2000s. Today, it’s one of the most recognizable entertainment properties on Earth, transcending the boundaries of just gaming — with its latest iteration, GTA VI, arriving this year with the highest grossing media launch ever. Day one sales of GTA VI generated over $3.79 billion, more than any other game or movie, amounting to the GDP of a small nation.

But more so than the money, GTA’s influence on gaming and culture at large is its true legacy. The open-world crime saga has informed the way video games are developed; its cinematic tone nailed an old Hollywood flavor that earlier games could only vaguely emulate; the freedom of choice in how to play inspired imitators of all kinds, from kid-friendly fare to direct copycats chasing the violent gangster gameplay.

Outside of the industry sphere, GTA became a touchstone for gaming as a concept. Think of any movie or show where characters are playing video games; it’s very likely the visual depiction will be a crudely rendered clone of GTA. A target of endless pearlclutching, politicians and advocates on both sides of the aisle have paraded the name as a leading cause of societal decay. To some, it’s a hedonistic simulacrum of sex and violence, encouraging players to indulge their darkest impulses.

And, sure, it’s a series where you can assault sex workers and commit mass shootings, but those options bely the point of Grand Theft Auto as a whole. At their best, the games serve as an intricately written parody of American culture — the greed, hypocrisy, and often downright idiocy that the country wears so proudly. In GTA, the American Dream is something to be gripped by force, and is delivered to audiences through caricature. It takes all the stories, media, and norms we love and reflects them back as satire. GTA doesn’t glorify crime, people do. It’s just laughing at us along the way.

To that end, not every GTA is so successful. The early top-down entries served more as arcade-style run-and-gunners that did little to admonish players to think beyond wanton destruction. But as technology evolved and storytelling devices matured, GTA began to better embody its role as Mean Streets meets South Park, telling exaggerated tales of criminality gone wrong to make audiences flinch — at least momentarily, before plotting their next heist.

In honor of GTA VI’s long-awaited release, Rolling Stone is ranking every Grand Theft Auto, from their humble Nineties-era origins to the modern blockbusters, both main games and expansions. Here’s every one, from worst to best.

Although the first two games in the series made appearances on the Game Boy Color, Grand Theft Auto Advance was the first original entry specifically developed for a Nintendo device. Blending the top-down overhead perspective of the OG installments with the mission structure of then-ubiquitous 3D versions, GTA Advance bridges the series’ oft-forgotten older design with more accessible gameplay.

As a prequel to 2001’s GTA III, players control a low-rent criminal named Mike whose dream of leaving Liberty City behind is blown to shreds by the mafia. Storywise, the plot comes through mostly via text and isn’t much to cling to. The handheld hardware of the Game Boy Advance doesn’t allow for much graphical fidelity, resulting in a game that looks worse than even the first PC entry, but is still commendable as a pocket-friendly way to play GTA.

To capitalize on the success of the original game, two expansions were green-lit as interim teasers before 1999’s full-fledged sequel. Grand Theft Auto: London 1969 released earlier that year as a standalone purchase, with 1961 following suit as a free download. Neither entry was groundbreaking, mostly recycling the gameplay and visuals of the base game with a Swingin’ Sixties finish. The duology is mostly fascinating for being the only GTA games set in a real city rather than fictional versions of American locales. The setting did result in one major innovation, however, with licensed music introduced to the franchise for the in-game radio stations — a feature that would become an essential part of GTA’s appeal moving forward.

Looking back, it’s hard to imagine how a game as simple as the original Grand Theft Auto kickstarted a media dynasty. Developed by Scottish studio DMA Design (now Rockstar North), the initial concept began as a simple cops and robbers sim called Race ‘n’ Chase, before being overhauled to focus on the more open-ended crime-oriented mission structure. Players choose from an assortment of unnamed protagonists to control, and must complete six linear levels spread across three cities (Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City), accruing a set number of points to progress.

Although seemingly basic in its top-down design, with a world composed mostly of tiny dot-like people and a handful of vehicle options, the first GTA built the foundation for everything else to come. Its six levels each serve as small sandboxes where players can choose to score cash as they see fit, and each city would later be fleshed out as fully realized urban sprawls in the 3D games. Like any of the series’ main characters, this freshman outing represents a humble start with great aspirations.

While the first batch of Game Boy Color and Advance releases proved that the series’ formula could be replicated for handheld with a few concessions, Liberty City Stories took things a step further — bringing a fully 3D GTA to the PlayStation Portable. Like GTA Advance, this all-new entry serves as a prequel to GTA III, albeit much more faithfully rendered, with graphics matching the home console version and even fully recorded voice acting for its cinematic cut scenes. In fact, it’s superior in some ways, incorporating gameplay features like changeable clothing and more intuitive camera controls. Once ported to the PlayStation 2, the game’s cracks began to show slightly; it’s a mostly inessential side quest for those who want more GTA III. But, in its initial portable incarnation, Liberty City Stories is a technical marvel.

The second spinoff developed for PlayStation Portable, Vice City Stories is yet another shining example of the impressive capabilities of Sony’s first foray into the handheld market. A prequel to 2002’s Vice City, it carries over the Eighties setting and includes an impressive voice cast for what’s essentially a mobile game, including Gary Busey, Miami Vice star Philip Michael Thomas, and even Phil Collins as himself.

Unlike its PSP predecessor, Vice City Stories does more than just replicate the console experience on-the-go, introducing some very ambitious new mechanics to the experience. The most prominent is the concept of empire building, where players must topple local local gang-affiliated businesses, then usurp control to create a network of private income sources, from brothels to protection rackets. Also like the previous game, Vice City Stories features a six-person multiplayer mode, although that feature was removed for the later PlayStation 2 rerelease.

While GTA as a series frequently pivots between settings and perspectives, Chinatown Wars marks some of the biggest departures for the franchise’s look and gameplay overall. The handheld game blends the top-down view of the early titles with a new cel-shaded aesthetic with thick character and environmental outlines reminiscent of a comic book. Initially designed for the dual-screen Nintendo DS, its gameplay features numerous touchscreen-based minigames — although both these controls and the stylized visuals were swapped out for the later PSP release.

But the most notable change in Chinatown Wars is a greater emphasis on drug-dealing, something that was controversial at release. As a Triad member, players can sell heroin, ecstasy, weed, cocaine and more — as well as strategize around different market conditions and geographical supply. It’s a murky system that goes deeper than most games in the series, which mostly ask the user to smuggle narcotics rather than peddle them directly.

At launch, GTA 2 was met with a mixed reception, mostly for failing to meaningfully innovate beyond the first game’s premise and design. But that’s not entirely true. The 1997 original did well to introduce the basics of open-ended mission structure and player choice, but its sequel perfected the formula for the pseudo-2D era.

Set in a fictional retro-futuristic city called Anywhere, U.S.A., GTA 2 sees players once again controlling a itty bitty protagonist as they conduct crime in a sequence of missions to progress through each level. This time, the setting is one large city divided by districts, and features rival gangs to work for, each at odds with each other. Balancing favor between the syndicates is key, and an increased level of environmental interactivity can lead to gang members engaging in their own immersive firefights with the police and each other. GTA 2 isn’t quite the quantum leap forward that its successor would be, but it’s a delightful piece of retro gaming nostalgia whose DNA can be seen in later indie games like Hotline Miami (2012).

Before the turn of the millennium, the GTA series had been a modest success, selling millions of units on PC and PlayStation, but it hadn’t quite hit the zeitgeist. GTA III would be the beginning of the dominant cultural force we know today. Rebooting the series’ narrative into a new continuity moving forward, it once again drops players into the New York-inspired setting of Liberty City — now rendered in full 3D — for an exponentially more cinematic experience.

For gamers, GTA III is a foundational text, popularizing many design choices and mechanics today’s player take for granted. Its urban open-world feels lived in, peppered with cars and pedestrians, each on their own loop that can be upended. Combat and gunplay, while simplistic by modern standards, are deeper than ever before thanks to the 3D leap; the ability to simultaneously drive a car and aim over-the-shoulder for a drive-by was astounding at the time. Most importantly, the first entry of this new era allowed Rockstar to fully realize the cinematic scope of what Grand Theft Auto always wanted to be. With elaborate cut scenes and voice acting from stars Frank Vincent, Debi Mazar, and Kyle MacLachlan, GTA III pioneered the blurring of lines between games and cinema. It’s basically gaming’s Mean Streets, a New Hollywood crime caper from which generations of developers would borrow from moving forward.

Much like the original game, 2008’s GTA IV received a duology of expansions that built on the base game’s foundation. But unlike the London content, The Lost and the Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony substantially add to the narrative and mechanics of their progenitor beyond being simple reskins.

Each expansion follows characters whose stories overlap with the main plot of GTA IV: biker Johnny Klebitz in the TLATD and bodyguard Luis Fernando Lopez in TBOGT. While both play similarly, each has distinct features beyond the base game. Johnny’s motorcycle club plays a huge role in his content, allowing players to call in the gang for backup when things get hairy. Luis’ gameplay isn’t notably different, but the story in his expansion is one of the very best in the series, celebrated at the time for its depiction of LGBTQ characters.

There was a time when game development was a much speedier process, with studios rapidly churning out quality sequels near annually. Rockstar themselves had a generational run from 2001 to 2004, dominating the conversation with the trifecta of GTA III, Vice City, and San Andreas. Even more impressive is how each game substantially improved on its predecessor despite wildly shifting apart in setting and tone.

Vice City falls squarely in the middle of the pack, transposing GTA III’s groundbreaking design into a Miami Vice and Scarface-inspired Eighties crime caper, complete with a lead character voiced by actor Ray Liotta. Control-wise, it’s not a huge leap forward; players still roam an open world hopping between main missions, side quests, and mini-games. What elevates Vice City is its pitch perfect take on Eighties Miami, depicting a greasy city soaked in neon, all set to one of the greatest video game soundtracks of all time.

Until very recently, GTA V was the series’ most ambitious entry to date. For many, it’s the definitive Grand Theft Auto experience — if only by default. The sole franchise entry in 13 years, GTA V was released for PlayStation 3, 4, and 5, selling a ludicrous 230 million copies over the course of its elongated lifespan.

In many ways, GTA V plays like a greatest hits of the series’ many ideas and mechanics, while modernizing its gameplay just enough to feel like an improvement over IV. Set in the fictional state of San Andreas (although set in a different “universe” than the 2004 title of that name), the story follows three unique protagonists, all with conflicting personalities and motives. Players will bounce between bank robber Michael De Santa, gangster Franklin Clinton, and psychopathic gunrunner Trevor Philips; their interwoven narrative bringing a slightly meandering Tarantino vibe to the otherwise kinetic plot, heavily inspired by Michael Mann’s Heat. Fans would be right to argue that GTA V deserves the top spot based on popularity alone, but looking back on the actual gameplay, it did little to substantially innovate over its direct predecessor. In 2013, GTA V’s gameplay arrived feeling dated, but was bolstered significantly by its feeling of limitless freedom and well-executed campaign story.

Although the series has many flavors, there’s a semblance of homogeny among the distinct crime syndicates throughout GTA. Regardless of the time period, there’s usually a depiction of the Italian mafia, Chinese Triads, maybe some Russians — with some depiction of Cuban and Haitian gangs cropping up in Vice City. 2004’s San Andreas broke served as a massive departure, centering on SoCal gang violence inspired by the Bloods and Crips.

While so much of the franchise’s inspiration seemingly comes from TV and movies (what better societal reflection, after all), San Andreas feels more informed by actual history, weaving in elements of real-life urban crises like the Nineties crack epidemic and the 1992 L.A. riots alongside storytelling lifted from films like John Singleton’s Boyz n the Hood. Outside of its unique setting and more impactful storytelling, one of San Andreas’ greatest contributions is an increased emphasis on the slice-of-life details and mini-games that shape the player character directly — something that is heavily prevalent in this year’s new entry, GTA VI.

Following a legendary run from 2001 to 2006, wherein five 3D GTA releases dominated home consoles and handhelds alike, the expectations for the next numbered entry in the franchise hit a fever pitch in 2008. Fortunately, GTA IV delivered the goods.

Resetting the table once again with a new vision of Liberty City, GTA IV traded in the sprawling map of San Andreas for a more densely packed and lively version of the series’ original locale. The story also eschewed any direct cinematic parallels to focus on a more original story leaning deeper into the satirical commentary of U.S. culture — specifically the American Dream. Unlike the thuggish mafioso types of games prior, GTA IV’s lead, Niko Bellic, is an ex-soldier and Eastern European immigrant, arriving in the states equally interested in revenge and a fresh start in the land of opportunity. Bringing in an outsider lends the game’s tone a sharper edge; this America is an alien place filled with unserious people.

Although its 2013 follow-up would offer better graphics and more features, GTA IV is essentially a perfected vision of what the 1997 original aimed to be, and stands less on the shoulders of other media to define its voice. This is the game that gave us Grand Theft Auto as we know it today.

For all its many elements, the defining feature of Grand Theft Auto as an idea is the emphasis on player freedom. Go anywhere, do whatever you want — that’s the ultimate promise. Except, every GTA is bound by the needs of a linear narrative. There’s a story to tell, players are just a part of it. But what if the story was entirely your own?

GTA Online launched as a 30-player online sandbox that emulated the mission structure of the base game while opening the door to infinite chaos. Rather than chasing down CPU-scripted non-playable characters, users are suddenly even squared against other humans who can react strategically (or erratically), turning the meta-gameplay of GTA to a new level without the constraints of a campaign story. But storytelling is still key, and following the game’s PC launch in 2015, modders cracked open GTA Online’s world with limitless potential. Now, it’s a platform where online roleplay reigns supreme, a second-life simulator where people go about their daily routines under fictional personas.

On streaming platforms, content creators have turned GTA RP into everything from reality TV to serial killer soap operas. It’s transcended individual gameplay to become its own ever-present world of entertainment to control or passively watch. While GTA V has kept selling throughout console generations, it’s clear that GTA Online has been the lifeblood of the series in its interim time between installments, and racked up billions in revenue that’s funded the series’ next big phase.

There are certain moments in time when a game changes everything. Pong had families enraptured around their cathode ray TVs; Tetris locked people into their screens on-the-go decades before smart phones became the norm. As a series, Grand Theft Auto’s had its fair share of these moments. GTA III stunned gamers with its open world, and V made it feel like it was possible live within a movie.

GTA VI might be the most incredible feat that Rockstar’s ever executed. From its opening moments, it’s instantly clear that there’s some insane technical alchemy going on. Its characters and environments are near photorealistic, and its world brimming with life. You can touch or do just about anything. In fact, players will spend their first few hours simply making coffee and painting their house.

But beyond the flashy graphics and complex coding of NPC and environmental scripts, the most immediate difference in GTA VI is how mature it feels — and not in the adults-only content kind of way. Its dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, aren’t jade caricatures of criminals pulled from pop media, but instead richly humanized characters with hopes and dreams. Although the game has all the hallmarks of a Grand Theft Auto underworld story, every written beat and player action serves to inform how the relationship between its leads blossoms. Arriving in 2026 to an American culture that’s well beyond parody, Rockstar’s decision to ground its story in the perspective of genuine people elevates it beyond anything the franchise was ever intended to be. GTA VI perfectly encompasses all that excess that Grand Theft Auto should have, while adding in a soul we never knew it so desperately needed.

#3267. Microsoft declares a Code Red in response to worst ever outage

The recent Microsoft 365 outage was the worst the service had ever experienced, with more than 80% of the company’s servers unresponsive at the worst point. The company has now declared a Code Red to address the way it prevents and responds to major failures in future.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and said that it’s urgently working on new approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour …

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

“Scattered across fragmented internal systems.” 😆

As someone who works in IT and manages Microsoft products, I thought that was their entire design philosophy.

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo says 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

#3266. These Are The Best In-Store Freebies Available on Black Friday

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Black Friday deals start showing up long before Black Friday actually arrives, and it's easy to shop most sales online without ever having to set foot in a store. But if you are willing to go early, stand in line, and navigate the crowds, you may be able to get some free stuff for your effort. Here are the freebies on offer this Black Friday.

The first 100 shoppers in line at Target on Black Friday will receive a gift card worth $25, $50, or $100, and one shopper at every store will get a $1,000 gift card. Stores open at 6 a.m., and tickets redeemable for free gift cards will be handed out starting approximately an hour before. Shoppers must exchange their tickets for their gift card within the first hour after doors open.

The first 200 shoppers at every Kohl's store on Black Friday will get a voucher for Kohl's Cash worth $5 to $100. Doors open at 5 a.m. If you show up on Saturday, Nov. 28 instead, you're eligible for a Sephora at Kohl's coupon (also worth $5 to $100).

If you're a MyLowe's Rewards member and you show up early on Black Friday, you could get one of several free buckets filled with products and coupons. The first 50 loyalty program members in line will receive a Black Friday Mystery Bucket, and four of those individuals will win one of the following grand prizes:

The next 100 members get a Golden Mini Bucket, which contains $5 in MyLowe's Monday and a 20% off coupon, among other things. The loyalty program is free to join, and doors open at 6 a.m.

The first 250 shoppers at Bass Pro Shops and Cabela's locations on Black Friday will receive a promo card worth between $10 and $500. The cards are valid Dec. 4 through 26, so you can't use them to shop that day.

JCPenney is running scheduled giveaways in stores throughout the day on Black Friday, so you could get free products even if you aren't there when doors open. If you line up at 5 a.m., you will get a peel-away card that is good for $10 off, $50 off, or $500 off your purchase, as well as a free Harry Potter mini snow globe. Additional giveaways will take place at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 5 p.m. for those in line.

Michaels is giving away 500 Countdown to Craftsmas advent calendars in stores on Black Friday while supplies last. The calendars come with store coupons, and some include other freebies and cash prizes up to a $100 gift card. One winner will receive a $10,000 nationwide grand prize.

Academy Sports is distributing bonus cards worth $20, $50, or $100 to the first 100 customers in line on Black Friday between 5 a.m. and 6 a.m. CT. Prize amounts will be randomly awarded among entrants. Academy Sports has locations across more than 20 states.

Best Buy's Black Friday promo isn't strictly free, but members of the My Best Buy rewards program (including the free tier) can purchase a $100 gift card for $60. There is a limit of one per person while supplies last, and cards can be used immediately, so you can take advantage of sales.

The first 30 shoppers at Golf Galaxy locations on Black Friday are eligible for instant prizes, including products, gift cards, and in-store services. One person per location will win a swag bag worth more than $500. Doors open at 7 a.m.

If you're among the first 500 shoppers at Fleet Farm when doors open at 5 a.m. on Black Friday, you'll receive a plush eagle toy. The company has also been running an "Orange Friday" event with in-store giveaways, though these have passed at most locations.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The Asics Superblast 3 is certainly an excellent running shoe, but this deal on the Superblast 2 is still tempting. It's a max-cushioned sneaker that feels great at almost any pace, and you can save $50 on the shoe in the Amazon sale right now.

#3264. 10 of the Best 'GTA 6' Cheat Codes, and How to Use Them

Cheat codes have long been a part of the Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, and the tradition continues with GTA 6. Not only does GTA 6 support cheats, but it also has a menu that lists all of them as well as instructions for unlocking them. However, you cannot fire up the game and start using cheats from the beginning. In fact, it requires quite a bit of work on your part. Here's how to unlock cheat codes in GTA 6, how to see the list of cheats, as well as the 10 best cheat codes in GTA 6.

Gone are the good old days when you could fire up GTA, enable god mode, unlimited ammo, no reload, spawn a jetpack, and run around the entire city destroying things at will. In GTA 6, you'll need to complete the main story to unlock the ability to use cheat codes. On top of that, you'll have to complete challenges of various difficulty levels to access specific cheat codes. Some of these cheats unlock the moment you finish the main story. Others, however, are quite challenging or time-consuming. For instance, unlimited reload requires you to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges.

Once you complete the main story in GTA 6, just go to in-game settings, and you'll see a new Cheats tab. This lists all 61 cheats and how to unlock them. You'll see the actual button combo for each cheat right after you complete the unlock requirement.

Unfortunately, there are some serious gameplay ramifications to using cheat codes in GTA 6. For starters, you can't save the game once you input even one cheat code. That's why it's best to save before you start using cheats, to avoid losing progress. Using cheat codes will also disable trophies and achievements in GTA 6.

To start using cheat codes in GTA 6, you'll have to get your character to pull up the smartphone by pressing the up arrow on the D-Pad. Then, hold L1+R1, and press the cheat's key combination on the D-Pad.

While there are a lot of cheat codes in GTA 6, these are 10 of the best, listed with the right key combination, and the condition to unlock them:

This cheat unlocks the moment you complete the main story in GTA 6. To use it, press up, right, down, left, up, left, down, right.

You unlock this cheat code after losing a three-star wanted level 25 times. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, down, up.

Lose a three-star wanted level 50 times to unlock this cheat. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, right, up.

This cheat unlocks the moment you wrap up the main story. Press this to unlock: down, up, up, down, up, down, up, down, up, right.

This is the third cheat that unlocks when you finish the main story. When you shoot or punch/kick characters, this cheat will launch them in the air. The key combination is: down, up, left, right, down, down, up, down

If you win 25 silver medals at shooting ranges, you can unlock infinite ammo in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, down.

To stop needing reloads, you need to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, up.

If you complete 100 workouts during your GTA 6 playthrough, you'll unlock the cheat that lets you instantly obtain body armor. Press this key combination to make it work: down, up, left, up, up, up, up, up, down, down.

This GTA 6 cheat allows you to change the weather at any time, and it unlocks when you finish the main story. Press this key combination to toggle it: down, right, up, down, right, up, right.

To spawn this cool emergency vehicle, you just need to discover the MTL Pumper in the game's progress menu. Use this key combination to spawn one: left, up, right, down, left, left, up, left.

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3262. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3260. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3256. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.
